title: Stage A2.1 — Imperfect, Reflexives, & Basic Subjunctive
description: Describe past habits and ongoing situations, talk about daily routines, make comparisons, and express wishes and commands using basic subjunctive. This stage introduces the imperfect tense alongside the preterite from A1.2.

grammar.title: Imperfect Tense (Pretérito Imperfecto) — Regular Verbs
grammar.content:
The imperfect describes past actions that were ongoing, habitual, or used for background descriptions. Unlike the preterite (A1.2), the imperfect doesn't show when something started or ended — it's the 'story-telling' tense used for setting scenes and describing repeated past actions.

For regular -AR verbs (like hablar), the endings are:
- yo: -aba
- tú: -abas
- él/ella/usted: -aba
- nosotros: -ábamos
- vosotros: -abais
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -aban

For regular -ER/-IR verbs (like comer, vivir), the endings are:
- yo: -ía
- tú: -ías
- él/ella/usted: -ía
- nosotros: -íamos
- vosotros: -íais
- ellos/ellas/ustedes: -ían
examples: De niño, jugaba en el parque todos los días. (As a child, I played in the park every day.)
Cuando éramos jóvenes, vivíamos en Barcelona. (When we were young, we lived in Barcelona.)
Mi abuela siempre cocinaba paella los domingos. (My grandmother always cooked paella on Sundays.)
A las ocho comía con mi familia. (At eight I used to eat with my family.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian imperfect endings (-am, -ai, -a, -am, -aţi, -au) are similar in function to Spanish -aba/-ía. Both describe ongoing or habitual past actions. The Spanish -aba ending is especially close to Romanian -am/-au in feeling: 'I was doing'.

grammar.title: Imperfect — The Three Irregulars (IR, VER, SER)
grammar.content:
Only three verbs are irregular in the imperfect, and they're among the most common in Spanish:

IR (to go): iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban
VER (to see): veía, veías, veía, veíamos, veíais, veían
SER (to be): era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran

VER is almost regular — it just takes the -ER endings (-ía) with an 'e' in the stem. IR and SER share the same forms, distinguished only by context.
examples: Siempre iba al cine los viernes. (I always went to the cinema on Fridays.)
De pequeño, veía muchas películas. (When I was little, I watched lots of movies.)
Él era muy inteligente. (He was very intelligent.)
Mi madre era profesora. (My mother was a teacher.)
grammar.aid_note: SER irregulars (era, eras, era...) are completely unlike the preterite (fui, fuiste, fue...). Don't confuse them! The Romanian 'era' (he/she was) is actually a cognate of Spanish 'era' — a nice memory boost for Romanian speakers.

grammar.title: Imperfect vs. Preterite: When to Use Which
grammar.content:
This is the key decision point for A2.1 learners. The preterite (from A1.2) and imperfect both describe the past, but differently:

Use IMPERFECT for:
- Habitual/repeated actions: 'De niño, nadaba todos los días.' (As a kid, I swam every day.)
- Ongoing background descriptions: 'Era una noche oscura y tormentosa.' (It was a dark and stormy night.)
- Age, time, weather in the past: 'Tenía 20 años. Eran las tres. Llovía.' (I was 20. It was three o'clock. It was raining.)
- Feelings and emotions in the past: 'Era feliz. Estaba cansado.' (I was happy. I was tired.)

Use PRETERITE for:
- Completed actions with a start/end: 'Ayer hablé con mi jefe.' (Yesterday I talked with my boss.)
- A series of completed actions: 'Me levanté, me duché y salí.' (I got up, showered, and left.)
- One-time specific past events: 'El año pasado fui a Italia.' (Last year I went to Italy.)

Both tenses can appear in the same sentence: 'Mientras llovía (imperfect), yo leía (imperfect) un libro. De repente, sonó el teléfono (preterite).' (While it was raining, I was reading a book. Suddenly, the phone rang.)

rows: Fue alto y rubio (described him as such)

examples: Cuando era niño, jugaba al fútbol. Todos los días. (When I was a child, I used to play soccer. Every day.)
Ayer jugué al fútbol. Ganamos 3-0. (Yesterday I played soccer. We won 3-0.)
Mientras ella cocinaba, él lavó los platos. (While she was cooking, he washed the dishes.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian also distinguishes between imperfect and aorist/preterite, but the distinction is less strictly taught in modern usage. The key intuition: imperfect = 'used to do / was doing', preterite = 'did (once, completed)'. In Romanian: 'făceam' (imperfect) vs 'făcei' (aorist/preterite).

grammar.title: Reflexive Verbs in the Imperfect (Daily Routines in the Past)
grammar.content:
Combine reflexive pronouns (me, te, se, nos, os, se) with imperfect conjugations to describe past daily routines. Reflexive pronouns stay BEFORE the conjugated verb (or attached to the infinitive when using a compound verb form).

Reflexive pronouns:
- me (myself)
- te (yourself, informal)
- se (himself/herself/itself/yourselves formal)
- nos (ourselves)
- os (yourselves, Spain informal)
- se (themselves/yourselves formal)

Example: 'Me despertaba a las siete.' (I used to wake up at seven.)
examples: Me despertaba a las seis de la mañana todos los días. (I used to wake up at six every day.)
Ellos se duchaban después de entrenar. (They used to shower after training.)
Nosotros nos acostábamos tarde los fines de semana. (We used to go to bed late on weekends.)
¿Te afeitabas por la mañana o por la noche? (Did you shave in the morning or at night?)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian reflexive verbs also use pronouns (mă, te, se, ne, vă, se) before the verb: 'mă trezeam' = 'me despertaba'. The structure is the same — just swap the verb conjugation.

grammar.title: Comparatives and Superlatives (Comparativos y Superlativos)
grammar.content:
Compare people, things, and ideas using comparatives and superlatives.

Comparative (more/less/as... as):
- más... que = more... than
- menos... que = less... than
- tan... como = as... as

Superlative (the most/the least):
- el/la más... = the most...
- el/la menos... = the least...

Irregular comparatives:
- bueno → mejor (better than)
- malo → peor (worse than)
- grande → mayor (older/greater than)
- pequeño → menor (younger/lesser than)

For age comparisons, mayor/menor are used instead of más/menos grande/pequeño when referring to age.

rows: Madrid es más grande que Sevilla.
Este libro es menos interesante que aquel.
Ella es tan inteligente como su hermano.
Él es el más alto de la clase.
Esta película es la menos divertida.

examples: Mi casa es más bonita que la tuya. (My house is prettier than yours.)
Ese examen fue más difícil que el anterior. (That exam was harder than the previous one.)
Mi hermano es mayor que yo. (My brother is older than me.)
Ella es la más inteligente de todos. (She is the smartest of all.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian comparatives follow the same pattern: 'mai bun' (better), 'mai frumos' (prettier), 'cel mai' (the most). Spanish 'más que' ≈ Romanian 'mai ... decât'. The irregulars (mejor, peor) are similar to Romanian 'mai bun' and 'mai rău'.

grammar.title: Basic Subjunctive in Fixed Expressions
grammar.content:
The subjunctive (subjuntivo) is a mood used to express wishes, doubts, emotions, and hypothetical situations. At A2.1, you'll mainly encounter it in fixed expressions — set phrases where the subjunctive is mandatory:

Wishes and blessings:
- ¡Que tengas un buen día! = Have a good day!
- ¡Que te vaya bien! = Good luck! (literally: may it go well for you)
- ¡Que descanses! = Rest well!

With querer/esperar + que (when the subject changes):
- Quiero que seas feliz. = I want you to be happy.
- Espero que llueva. = I hope it rains.

Common fixed expressions:
- Ojalá (que)... = I hope that... / God willing...
- Es importante que... = It's important that...
- Mejor que... = Better if...

The present subjunctive yo form is built by taking the yo present indicative form and switching the ending: -o → -e for -AR, -o → -a for -ER/-IR:
- hablar → hablo → hable
- comer → como → coma
- vivir → vivo → viva
examples:
¡Que tengas un excelente día! (Have an excellent day!)
Ojalá llueva mañana. (I hope it rains tomorrow.)
Quiero que tú vengas a mi fiesta. (I want you to come to my party.)
Espero que esté bien. (I hope he/she is okay.)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian uses a similar 'optative' mood for wishes: 'Să ai o zi bună!' = '¡Que tengas un buen día!' The 'să' particle marks the subjunctive optative. This makes the Spanish subjunctive much more natural for Romanian speakers than for English speakers, whose language doesn't have a subjunctive mood in everyday speech.

grammar.title: Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns (Introduction)
grammar.content:
Object pronouns replace nouns to avoid repetition. There are two types:

Direct Object Pronouns (replaces the DIRECT object — the person/thing directly affected by the verb):
- me (me)
- te (you, informal)
- lo/la (him/her/it — masculine/feminine)
- nos (us)
- los/las (them — masculine/feminine)
- les (them — formal, Spain)

Indirect Object Pronouns (replaces the INDIRECT object — the person FOR WHOM the action is done):
- me (to/for me)
- te (to/for you, informal)
- le (to/for him/her/you formal)
- nos (to/for us)
- les (to/for them/you formal plural)
- os (to/for you plural, Spain informal)

Pronoun placement: BEFORE the conjugated verb, or attached to the END of an infinitive/gerund.

Example: 'Veo la película' → 'La veo.' (I see the movie → I see it.)
'Le doy el libro a María' → 'Le doy el libro.' (I give the book to María → I give her the book.)

rows: Me veo. / Me da el libro.
Te veo. / Te da el libro.
Nos vemos. / Nos da el libro.
Os veo. / Os da el libro.

examples: ¿Ves a tu hermano? — Sí, lo veo. (Do you see your brother? — Yes, I see him.)
María me llama cada día. (María calls me every day.)
Le di un regalo a mi madre. (I gave a gift to my mother.)
¿Puedes ayudarme? (Can you help me?)
grammar.aid_note: Romanian has a similar system: 'mă/te/îl/îi/ne/vă/îi' for object pronouns. The Spanish lo/la distinction (masculine/feminine) is similar to Romanian îl/îi. Romanian speakers should find object pronouns much easier than English speakers.

vocabulary.source: to be happy / to be glad

pronunciation.title: Stress Patterns with Imperfect Endings
pronunciation.content:
The imperfect endings all carry the stress on a predictable syllable:

-AR verbs (-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban): stress is always on the -a- of the ending. 'HablaBA', 'hablaBAs', 'hablaBA', 'hablaBAMOS' (wait — actually: hablÁbamos has the stress on the first 'a' of the ending), hablÁBais, hablABan.

-ER/-IR verbs (-ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían): stress is always on the í. 'ComÍA', 'comÍAS', 'comÍA', 'comÍAMOS', 'comÍAIS', 'comÍAN'.

All imperfect endings are naturally stressed on their first syllable. Remember the accent on nosotros: hablÁbamos, comÍamos (the accent mark on the 'a' and 'í' shows where the stress falls).

examples.source: stress on the first Í: ve-Ía-MOS

pronunciation.aid_note: Romanian stress is more flexible and often falls on the last syllable. Spanish imperfect endings are very regular — the stress always hits the ending syllable, never the stem. This makes them easier to pronounce than Romanian imperfect forms.

pronunciation.title: The Vowel Sound in Imperfect Endings
pronunciation.content:
The imperfect endings contain only two vowel sounds, both of which are simple and consistent:

-AR verbs: the 'a' in all endings (-aba, -abas, -aba, -ábamos, -abais, -aban) is the same clear 'a' sound, like the 'a' in 'father.'
-ER/-IR verbs: the 'í' contains the stressed 'i' vowel sound, like the 'ee' in 'see' but shorter and crisper.

Important: Spanish 'i' and 'e' are never diphthongs. They are pure, single vowel sounds. 'Comía' is pronounced 'ko-MEE-ah' (three distinct syllables), NOT 'ko-MEE-ya' or 'ko-MEE-uh' as English speakers might assume.
pronunciation.aid_note: Romanian also has pure vowel sounds (ă, â, î, â, e, i, o, u) — no diphthongs like English 'ay' or 'ow'. Spanish speakers of Romanian will find this aspect very natural. The key difference: Spanish 'e' is more open (like 'bed') while Romanian 'e' is slightly more closed.

exercises.question: What does the imperfect tense describe?
options: Completed actions with a clear end
exercises.explanation: The imperfect describes habitual or ongoing past actions — things that 'used to happen' or 'were happening' without a defined endpoint.

exercises.question: Which ending is the imperfect 'yo' form for -AR verbs?
exercises.explanation: -AR verbs take -aba in the yo imperfect form: hablaba, trabajaba, estudiaba.

exercises.question: Complete: 'De niño, yo ____ (jugarse) en el parque todos los días.' (As a child, I used to play in the park every day.)
exercises.explanation: 'Me jugaba' — the reflexive pronoun 'me' + imperfect 'jugaba' of 'jugar.' The reflexive is needed for the sense of 'playing (oneself)' in this context.

exercises.question: What is the imperfect of 'ir' for 'nosotros'?
exercises.explanation: 'Íbamos' — IR is one of three imperfect irregulars. It carries an accent mark on the í to show the stress.

exercises.question: What is the imperfect of 'ser' for 'ellos'?
exercises.explanation: 'Eran' — SER is an imperfect irregular: era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran. Don't confuse with the conditional 'serían' (they would be).

exercises.question: Complete: 'Cuando era pequeña, mi madre ____ (cocinar) paella los domingos.' (When I was little, my mother used to cook paella on Sundays.)
exercises.explanation: 'Cocinaba' — regular -AR verb in the imperfect. The -aba ending for él/ella/usted.

exercises.question: Which sentence uses the imperfect correctly?
options: De niño, jugaba al fútbol todos los días.
El año pasado jugué al fútbol.
exercises.explanation: 'De niño, jugaba al fútbol todos los días' uses the imperfect for a habitual past action. The other sentences use preterite or present.

exercises.question: What is the imperfect of 'ver' for 'yo'?
exercises.explanation: 'Veía' — VER is an imperfect irregular that follows the regular -ER endings (-ía, -ías, -ía...) but with a 've-' stem.

exercises.question: Complete: 'Nosotros ____ (vestirse) todos los días a las siete.' (We used to get dressed every day at seven.)
exercises.explanation: 'Nos vestíamos' — reflexive 'nos' + imperfect of vestirse. The -ir verb takes the -ía ending for nosotros: vestíamos.

exercises.question: Match each profession with its Spanish translation:
exercises.explanation: These are common professions you'll need when describing people's work. Note gender agreement: la enfermera (feminine), la abogada (feminine).

exercises.question: Complete: 'La casa ____ (ser) muy grande y ____ (tener) un jardín hermoso.' (The house was very big and had a beautiful garden.)
exercises.explanation: 'Era tenía' — SER and TENER in the imperfect. 'Era' (was) for description, 'tenía' (had) for possession.

exercises.question: Which word means 'taller' in Spanish (comparative)?
exercises.explanation: 'Más alto' means taller (more tall). The structure is 'más + adjective + que': 'Él es más alto que yo.'

exercises.question: Complete: 'Este libro es ____ interesante que aquel.' (This book is more interesting than that one.)
exercises.explanation: 'Más interesante' — the comparative structure 'más + adjective + que.'

exercises.question: What is the irregular comparative of 'bueno'?
exercises.explanation: 'Mejor' is the irregular comparative of bueno (better). 'Más bueno' is sometimes used colloquially but 'mejor' is correct.

exercises.question: Which of these uses the subjunctive correctly?
exercises.explanation: 'Ojalá llueva mañana' uses the subjunctive correctly. 'Ojalá' always triggers the subjunctive. 'Viene' → 'vengas' in subjunctive.

exercises.question: Complete: '¡Que tengas ____ día!' (Have a ____ day!) — subjunctive wish for someone.
exercises.explanation: '¡Que tengas un buen día!' uses the subjunctive 'tengas' (from tener) after 'que.' For wishes, use the subjunctive: que + subjunctive.

exercises.question: What does the direct object pronoun 'lo' replace?
exercises.explanation: 'Lo' replaces a masculine singular direct object: 'Veo el libro → Lo veo.' 'La' would replace a feminine one.

exercises.question: Complete: '¿Ves a Juan? — Sí, ____ veo cada día.' (Do you see Juan? — Yes, I see him every day.)
exercises.explanation: 'Lo' replaces 'Juan' (masculine singular direct object). The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb.

exercises.explanation: These emotions are essential for describing how people felt in the past (using imperfect of estar + past participle: estaba cansado, estaba triste).

exercises.explanation: These furniture items are commonly used when describing houses and daily routines.

exercises.question: Complete the imperfect tense conjugation table for the regular -AR verb HABLAR:
exercises.explanation: The imperfect of hablar follows the regular -AR pattern: hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban.

exercises.question: Complete the imperfect tense conjugation table for the irregular verb SER:
exercises.explanation: SER is one of only three irregular imperfect verbs: era, eras, era, éramos, erais, eran.

exercises.question: Complete the imperfect tense conjugation table for the irregular verb IR:
exercises.explanation: IR is one of only three irregular imperfect verbs: iba, ibas, iba, íbamos, ibais, iban. Note the accent on íbamos.

exercises.question: Complete: 'De niño, ____ (deber) estudiar mucho pero ____ (querer) jugar.' (As a child, I had to study a lot but I wanted to play.)
exercises.explanation: 'Debía quería' — both verbs in the imperfect. 'Debía' shows past obligation (I had to), 'quería' shows past desire (I wanted to). Both are imperfect because they describe repeated past states.

exercises.question: Which verb form is the subjunctive of 'tener' (yo)?
exercises.explanation: 'Tenga' is the present subjunctive yo form: take the yo indicative (tengo), drop the -o, add -a for -ER verbs: tenga.
